journey.arc: The thesis records a one-year MPhil in the Popelier group (2017-2018) whose open brief was to 'extend the applicability of the FFLUX force field' (p. 21). FFLUX replaces fixed-form valence terms with kriging models of quantum atoms and uses high-order multipoles for electrostatics, but after a decade it had only optimised a single water molecule and capped glycine (p. 86). The author first audits FFLUX and reports three negative results: no intermolecular polarisation, 'extrapolation collapse' outside the training set, and the curse of dimensionality (Ch. 3). Two methodological developments follow. The first began as a search for a cheap exchange term to model peptide bonds, then pivoted into a study of the delocalization index as a bond-order indicator, benchmarked on ~200 molecules and published in Chemical Science (Ch. 4). The second, symmetry-adapted kriging, builds permutational symmetry into the models with a group-theoretic kernel and a pivot heuristic, implemented in DL_FFLUX and tested on four small molecules (Ch. 5). The polarisation problem is left open. Order of stages follows the thesis narrative; the author says the path 'might perhaps look sinuous' (p. 21) and gives no dated chronology, so actual order of work is not established.

stages.title: Orientation: the force-field problem and the FFLUX brief
stages.question: Why do biomolecular force fields still fail, and how could the group's machine-learned FFLUX force field be extended?
stages.approach: Argues force fields, not sampling, limit simulation (p. 19-20); reviews MD, intermolecular forces, polarisable force fields, Quantum Chemical Topology, Gaussian process regression and FFLUX history (Ch. 2).
stages.outcome_note: Background stage: sets scope and tools; no experiment.
stages.why_next: FFLUX had reached only single-water and capped-glycine optimisation after a decade (p. 86), so the author asks what the main challenges are before scaling up (p. 87).

stages.title: Formalise FFLUX: architecture, forces, training pipeline
stages.question: What exactly is FFLUX's potential, how are atomic forces obtained, and how are the kriging models trained?
stages.approach: Writes E_FFLUX = E_IQA + E_electrostatic + E_dispersion; defines atomic-local-frame features; derives forces by chain rule through the rotation matrix and the multipole interaction tensors; documents the GAIA pipeline (TYCHE, Gaussian 09, AIMAll, NORMART, FEREBUS, DL_FFLUX).
stages.outcome_note: Presents and derives existing group machinery; numerical verification of the force formulae is referred to ref. [231] (p. 98).
stages.why_next: With the formulation written down, the author tests it against three physical and mathematical questions (3.4).

stages.title: Test 1: is intermolecular polarisation negligible?
stages.question: Can FFLUX's geometry-only multipoles stand in for polarised electrostatics in a condensed environment?
stages.approach: Five snapshots of a 5-water cluster (BP86/Def2SVP BOMD at 600 K, RI-MP2/cc-pVTZ optimisation); compares electrostatic energy from in-vacuo monomer multipoles with energy from cluster multipoles, up to quadrupole, with AIMAll.
stages.outcome_note: Negative result: ~400 kcal/mol electrostatic error, cluster charges shift 0.10 +/- 0.05 e, and conformer ordering is wrong (p. 103). Not fixed; self-consistent polarisation is suggested as future work (p. 104).
stages.why_next: Left as an open conceptual limit: FFLUX is 'multipolar' rather than polarisable. Neither Ch. 4 nor Ch. 5 addresses it, and Ch. 6 does not return to it.

stages.title: Test 2: what happens outside the training set?
stages.question: How does a kriging potential behave when a simulation leaves the region it was trained on?
stages.approach: Mathematical argument that the correlation vector goes to zero and the prediction tends to the process mean; single-water model (500 TYCHE points, B3LYP/aug-cc-pVTZ); stretched-bond dissociation curve; Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo of 2,500 steps.
stages.outcome_note: Negative result ('extrapolation collapse'): potential goes flat beyond the training range and forces vanish; MC energy stalls at -76.4166 hartree after ~1,000 steps (Fig. 3.5). Two remedies considered and set aside (pp. 108-109).
stages.why_next: No simple fix exists, which makes models that cover more of configuration space cheaply attractive; Ch. 5 cites this section as motivation (p. 148).

stages.title: Test 3: does the model scale to a flexible molecule?
stages.question: Do published capped-glycine kriging models give sensible energies on geometries that a finite-temperature simulation would visit?
stages.approach: 200 RDKit conformers, MMFF94 relaxation and RMSD pruning, 10 lowest kept; B3LYP/apc-1 optimisation plus 200 fs BOMD at 600 K (ORCA) gives 2,000 test geometries; evaluates the published ~0.5 GB model.
stages.outcome_note: Negative result: ~600 kcal/mol mean error, bimodal prediction distribution, minima not ranked (Fig. 3.8). Author blames a 51-dimensional space sampled by about a thousand points and criticises same-method test sets.
stages.why_next: Calls for fewer training points and representative test sets (p. 113). Ch. 4 also avoids a two-monomer exchange model because of this problem (p. 116), and Ch. 6 says Ch. 5 was motivated by it (p. 183).

stages.title: Pivot: from an exchange term for the peptide bond to the delocalization index
stages.question: How can FFLUX represent covalent (exchange) interaction between monomers, for example the peptide bond?
stages.approach: Rejects a harmonic bond (undoes FFLUX's purpose) and a kriged V_xc (six-dimensional integrals and curse of dimensionality). Proposes the delocalization index as a first-order approximation to V_xc using only 3-D integrals, and proves this for arbitrary wavefunctions; adopts Müller's approximation for correlated 2-RDMs.
stages.outcome_note: 'Soon acquired a dimension of its own' as a bond-order study (p. 116). Suitability of DI as an FFLUX exchange potential is explicitly left as future work (p. 117).
stages.why_next: Before using DI anywhere, the author checks the approximation used to compute it (j7) and how DI behaves in ordinary chemistry (j8).

stages.title: Check Müller's approximation against the full 2-RDM
stages.question: Is the Müller approximation accurate enough to compute DIs for correlated wavefunctions?
stages.approach: 21 small molecules at CCSD/6-311++G(2d,2p): full 2-RDM from pySCF plus PROMOLDEN versus AIMAll's Müller approximation.
stages.outcome_note: Most directly bonded pairs within 5%, but N2 (11.4%), HCN C-N (10.1%) and F2 (34.1%) worse; non-bonded DIs underestimated 20-70% except H-bonds, which are overestimated (Table 4.1). Full 2-RDM took ~2 weeks vs ~10 h.
stages.why_next: Accepted as a qualitative tool: HF values serve as the baseline and CCSD/Müller as a lower bound for weak interactions (p. 129).

stages.title: Survey ~200 molecules: does DI behave like a bond order?
stages.question: Do delocalization indices reproduce Lewis bond orders and the subtler effects of practical chemistry?
stages.approach: ~200 organic and inorganic molecules (28 inorganic) at HF and CCSD/6-311++G(2d,2p) with Gaussian 09 and AIMAll; 14,756 HF DI entries; plateau analysis, k-means, HF vs CCSD comparison, homologous series and resonance examples.
stages.outcome_note: DIs cluster near single/aromatic/double values (C-C ~1.0/1.4/1.8), HF is closest to Lewis, correlation lowers bonded DIs and raises weak ones, inductive and resonance effects are recovered; polar bonds fall below formal order.
stages.why_next: Having tested only well-known patterns, the author applies DI to disputed exotic bonding (j9).

stages.title: Apply DI to exotic bonding: N8, planar carbon, an iron complex
stages.question: Can delocalization indices clarify bonding in disputed or unusual molecules?
stages.approach: N8 (EEE and EZE isomers), dilithium cyclopropane (planar tetracoordinate carbon), and (eta4-C4H6)Fe(CO)3 (B3LYP geometry, HF and CCSD single points).
stages.outcome_note: N8: proposes a pentavalent-nitrogen Lewis structure that disagrees with the discoverers' ionic NBO picture; Li2-cyclopropane: no revision needed; Fe complex: total DI ~1.7 consistent with a double bond. Metal complexes otherwise avoided because Müller cannot handle static correlation (p. 141).
stages.why_next: Closes the DI thread (published as Chem. Sci. 2018, App. A). The thesis then turns to the sampling problem raised in 3.4 (Ch. 5); Ch. 6 states that link (p. 183).

stages.title: Make kriging respect permutational symmetry
stages.question: How can a kriging potential recognise that relabelled identical atoms are the same molecule?
stages.approach: Reviews symmetry-adapted features and models (5.1); uses finite group theory and faithful representations; builds a kernel summed over group images of each training point; proves invariance by the rearrangement theorem with an isotropic kernel and isometric representations.
stages.outcome_note: Invariance is proven, but in pure form it costs N kernel evaluations per training point, O(NM) (p. 162), and needs FEREBUS changes because symmetry-related weights are shared.
stages.why_next: A heuristic is needed to avoid the N-fold cost (j11).

stages.title: Cut the cost: pivot heuristic and DL_FFLUX implementation
stages.question: Can symmetry be built in without paying for N kernel evaluations?
stages.approach: Splits configuration space into symmetry-equivalent regions; chooses a pivot (usually a PES minimum); applies each representation matrix to the query geometry and keeps the image with minimum Kabsch RMSD to the pivot. Implemented as fflux_symmetry_transformation in DL_POLY FFLUX, leaving feature and force code untouched (App. B).
stages.outcome_note: Cost drops to O(M). The RMSD metric is a heuristic; a metric from first principles is left to future work (p. 165).
stages.why_next: Tested on water, ammonia, methanol and acetaldehyde (j12).

stages.title: Test on water, ammonia, methanol and acetaldehyde
stages.question: Does symmetry-adapted kriging give consistent curves and optimisations when trained on one symmetry region only?
stages.approach: Water and NH3 dissociation curves (100 MP2/cc-pVTZ points, MolecularSAGPR on scikit-learn); methanol (600 points) and acetaldehyde (900 points) in DL_FFLUX, TYCHE at 3000 K from one seed; 6,000 test geometries (1,000 x 6 permutations) minimised for 1,500 steps.
stages.outcome_note: All symmetry-adapted runs reach the expected minimum (methanol mean RMSD 0.002 +/- 0.004 A); baseline runs mostly end in wrong structures. One trajectory shows a boundary effect (p. 173). Only one P(3) symmetry centre is tested.
stages.why_next: Conclusions (Ch. 6): the method is ready to be deployed and will go into the next FFLUX version (p. 181).

stages.title: Synthesis: two methodological contributions
stages.question: What does the work amount to?
stages.approach: Restates the DI work (cheap exchange proxy, Müller validation, bond-order clustering, exotic cases) and symmetry-adapted kriging (group-theoretic kernel plus pivot heuristic).
stages.outcome_note: Polarisation and extrapolation collapse from Ch. 3 are not revisited in Ch. 6; Ch. 1 promises 'future lines of work' (p. 21) but Ch. 6 has no such list.
stages.why_next: End of the thesis. Author hands over DI as a bond-order indicator and SAGPR as a tool ready to deploy (p. 185).

contributions.text: Critical appraisal of FFLUX with three simple numerical tests: neglected intermolecular polarisation, extrapolation collapse, and the curse of dimensionality.

Delocalization index shown to be a first-order approximation to the exchange-correlation energy for an arbitrary wavefunction, benchmarked (Müller approximation), surveyed over ~200 molecules and applied to exotic bonding; published in Chemical Science 2018.
Symmetry-adapted kriging: group-theoretic kernel, pivot heuristic, implementation in DL_POLY FFLUX, tests on four small molecules.
Written derivation of FFLUX atomic forces and a description of the training pipeline (numerical verification cited from earlier work).

claims.text: Very long (>100 microsecond) simulations on special-purpose hardware showed proteins drifting from native structures; the cited authors read this as force fields, not sampling, being limiting.
The thesis records the author's 2017-2018 MPhil year in the Popelier group under an open brief.

FFLUX (formerly QCTFF) grew from rigid-molecule multipolar simulations of HF and water to kriging-predicted conformation-dependent multipoles, after kriging outperformed neural networks in group comparisons.
By 2018 FFLUX's maximum demonstrations were optimisations of one water molecule and of capped glycine.
Abstract: FFLUX replaces fixed-form valence potentials with non-parametric regression and uses high-order multipolar electrostatics, aiming at ligand-receptor energetics.
E_FFLUX = E_IQA + E_electrostatic + E_dispersion: E_IQA is a kriged atomic energy, dispersion is Lennard-Jones, electrostatics use kriged multipoles up to hexadecapole.
FFLUX assumes charge transfer can be modelled by geometry changes alone.
Features live in an Atomic Local Frame, removing six translational and rotational degrees of freedom; the frame is set by the heaviest and second-heaviest bonded neighbours (CIP rules for ties).

Atomic forces follow from the chain rule through the ALF rotation matrix (internal forces) and through derivatives of the multipole interaction tensors (electrostatic forces); numerical checks are cited from ref. [231].
Training runs through GAIA: TYCHE geometries, Gaussian 09, AIMAll integration, NORMART rotation to the ALF, FEREBUS training, then DL_FFLUX.
In FFLUX the charge distribution depends only on molecular geometry, so polarisation is intramolecular only; two same-geometry molecules in different environments get identical multipoles.
In five water-cluster conformers, using in-vacuo rather than cluster multipoles gave an electrostatic error of about 400 kcal/mol, and cluster charges shifted by 0.10 +/- 0.05 e.

Unpolarised electrostatics cannot rank two conformers: the difference is ~8 kcal/mol with each treatment but of opposite sign (~16 kcal/mol in total); the conclusion rounds this to 'about 20' (p. 114).
As features leave the training range the GP prediction tends to the process mean, so the potential is flat and forces are zero ('extrapolation collapse').
In a single-water Metropolis-Hastings run, the energy sticks at -76.4166 hartree after ~1,000 of 2,500 steps and the molecule distorts unphysically.
Two remedies are set aside: a feature-dependent mean (classical bond potential) cancels the non-parametric benefit, and dense sampling is costly and often impossible via the curse of dimensionality.
A published capped-glycine model (~0.5 GB) tested on 2,000 B3LYP/apc-1 BOMD geometries gives a ~600 kcal/mol mean error and does not rank minima.
The 51-dimensional feature space is extremely sparse for a training set of about a thousand examples.
Earlier assessments built test sets by the same method as training sets (selection bias), and published simulations show optimisation to minima but not the energetics along trajectories.
Three open challenges: neglect of intermolecular polarisation, extrapolation collapse and the curse of dimensionality.
In current FFLUX monomers interact only through electrostatics and dispersion, so covalent exchange (e.g. the peptide bond) is missing.

Kriging V_xc directly needs six-dimensional integrals over irregular boundaries and models of two monomers' coordinates (curse of dimensionality); a harmonic potential would undo FFLUX's aims; so the DI is proposed as a cheaper proxy.
Integrating the exchange-correlation pair density gives N = sum of localization indices plus sum of delocalization indices, splitting an atom's electron pairs into localized and delocalized sets.
The DI is a first-order (charge-charge-like) approximation to V_xc for an arbitrary wavefunction and needs 3-D rather than 6-D integrals.
Müller's approximation estimates the correlated 2-RDM from the 1-RDM; it violates the Pauli principle in general, and p = 0 minimises the violation.

On 21 small molecules, most directly bonded DIs from CCSD/Müller are within 5% of full-2-RDM CCSD; N2 (11.4%), HCN C-N (10.1%) and F2 (34.1%) are worse; non-bonded DIs are underestimated 20-70% except hydrogen bonds, which are overestimated.
The full CCSD 2-RDM needed ~2 weeks on a 12-CPU node versus ~10 h on 4 cores for AIMAll with Müller.
HF DIs recover Lewis bond orders (H2 1.000, N2 ~3.04, O2 2.27); CCSD/Müller lowers bonded DIs (H2 0.844, N2 2.310, O2 1.615) and raises weak ones (Ne2 0.005 to 0.009, Ar2 0.002 to 0.015).
HF and CCSD/Müller DIs correlate strongly (Pearson 0.938 over 1,666 bonds).

The ~200-molecule database holds 14,756 HF DI entries; C-C DIs plateau near 1.0, 1.4 and 1.8; C-O near 0.8, ~1.2 (aldehydes) and ~1.4 (ketones); weak interactions separate sharply from bonds near 0.5.
k-means with three centroids on (DI, distance) pairs recovers the plateaus.
DI reflects bond polarity (N2 3.043 vs HCN C-N 2.340), inductive decay along homologous series, and resonance (phenoxide C-O 1.070).
For N8, DIs and QTAIM charges below 0.14 e argue against Hirshberg et al.'s ionic NBO structure and for a pentavalent-nitrogen Lewis structure.
In dilithium cyclopropane (planar tetracoordinate carbon) C-C DIs are 0.98-1.11 and the C-Li DI (0.197) is close to LiH (0.193), so the Li bonds are ionic and no concept needs revising.
In (eta4-C4H6)Fe(CO)3, DI(terminal C, Fe) = 0.469 versus 0.292 for the central carbon at HF (0.788 vs 0.286 at CCSD); the total ~1.7 is a double bond, despite no bond path to terminal carbons.
The DI is proposed as a general bond-order indicator; whether it works as an FFLUX exchange potential is left as future work.
Chapter 4 was published as Outeiral et al., Chem. Sci. 2018, 9, 5517-5529; the author did the vast majority of calculations and all of the analysis.

The six permutation-equivalent methanol minima share one Hamiltonian, but ordinary kriging trained on one seed either collapses or optimises to unphysical structures, for example ignoring the rotation barrier.
Prior work uses permutation-invariant features (Behler-Parrinello, bispectrum, SOAP, Coulomb matrices) or invariant models (invariant polynomials).
A kernel summed over the group images of each training point gives an invariant GP predictor, proved via the rearrangement theorem, an isotropic kernel and isometric representations.
Pure symmetry-adapted kriging needs N kernel evaluations per training point (O(NM)), so it saves nothing by itself.
Heuristic: map the query into the modelled region by choosing the symmetry image with minimum Kabsch RMSD to a pivot (a PES minimum); cost drops to O(M).
Implemented as fflux_symmetry_transformation in two_body_forces.f90 of DL_POLY FFLUX, reading matrices from MATRICES.txt; feature and force routines unchanged.
With 100 MP2/cc-pVTZ points per curve, SAGPR reproduces the stretch of every symmetry-equivalent bond in H2O and NH3, while ordinary GP fails on relabelled bonds.

Methanol (600 training points, 6,000 test geometries): symmetry-adapted minimisations converge to the B3LYP/aug-cc-pVTZ minimum (mean RMSD 0.002 +/- 0.004 A); baseline runs mostly end in wrong structures.
Acetaldehyde (900 training points) shows the same pattern as methanol.
Symmetry adaptation lets the training set shrink about six-fold relative to adding all permuted copies.
Conclusions claim DI is proven to be a first-order V_xc approximation, Müller is valid to ~10% for directly bonded atoms, and SAGPR is ready to deploy.

observations.text: Polarisation error in water clusters is ~16 kcal/mol in total on p. 103 but 'about 20 kcal/mol' on p. 114 (checked on page image).
Conclusions say Müller is within a 10% error bound for directly bonded atoms (p. 183); Table 4.1 lists F-F at 34.1% and N-N at 11.4% (p. 128), though the text treats F2 and HF as exceptions.
Benzaldehyde C-O DI: thesis p. 137 and the Fig. 4.4 caption give 0.798; the published paper's text gives benzaldehyde 1.297 and 0.798 for propanol (p. 196, checked on page image).
Chapter 1 promises that Chapter 6 outlines 'future lines of work' (p. 21); Chapter 6 contains no such list. Future-work remarks are scattered in 3.4, 4 (p. 117) and 5.3.1.
Pages 187-200 are a copy of the journal paper and carry the journal's pagination (5497-5529); thesis page numbers there are counted, not printed.
